Essay:

More Than One Voice

Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide if she should take a job in a different city. First she asked her mom, and her mom told her to stay close to home. If Dana stopped right there she would of said no to the job. But she kept asking people. She talked to four people total and she changed her mind two times before she finally picked. I watched the whole thing happen and it showed me that asking a few people for advice is better than asking only one.

The first reason is that each person only sees part of what is going on. Dana's mom kept talking about how lonely it is in a new city. She moved one time when she was younger and she hated it, so that's what she thinks about. Dana's old manager talked about the money and the job title, because thats the stuff he knows about. Then Dana had a friend who already lived in that city, and she told her about rent and traffic and how long it took her to make friends there. Nobody was wrong. But nobody knew everything either. When Dana put all of the answers together it was kind of like a map that was almost finished. One person gives you one side of it. A bunch of people show you the parts you couldn't see by yourself.

The second reason is that people want things for themselves, even the people who love you. Dana's mom wanted her to live nearby. That is a nice thing to want, but it's not the same thing as what is best for Dana's job. It's like when you go to buy a phone and the guy at the store tells you which one to get. He might be telling the truth, but he also gets paid more if you buy it. If he is the only person you ask, you can't tell which part is real advice and which part is him wanting money. But if you also ask a friend who has that phone, and you look up what a person who fixes phones says, then it evens out. When three people who all want different things tell you the same answer, you can trust it a lot more than just one of them.

The third reason is that it actually helps when people disagree. Two people that Dana really respected told her the opposite thing, so she had to figure out why. It turned out her manager thought she wanted to move up fast at work, and her friend thought she cared more about having free time. That made Dana ask herself a question she never asked before, which was what does she even want for the next five years. Doctors know about this too. When somebody needs surgery, a lot of times they are told to get a second opinion from another doctor. If the second doctor agrees, the person feels better about it. If the second doctor doesn't agree, then the person knows it is not as simple as it sounded, and you would want to know that before they cut you open.

Some people might say that asking too many people just makes you confused. That is true sometimes. Ten opinions could be worse than two, and some people keep asking just so they don't have to decide. But you are not supposed to count votes. Dana didn't take the job because three out of four people said to. She took it because all the talking showed her what she cared about and what could go wrong. Then she picked for herself.

In conclusion, asking more than one person doesn't mean other people decide for you. It just gives you more facts and better questions, and it keeps one person from pushing you their way. Dana has lived in her new city for eight months now. She still calls her mom every Sunday.
